entries.title: Goodreads finally supports both half-star ratings
entries.summary: You can now rate books on Goodreads from 0.25 to 5.0 stars (including popular intermediate values like 3.5, 4.5, 3.75, and 4.25). The post Goodreads finally supports both half-star ratings first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Goodreads officially supports both half-star (0.5) and quarter-star (0.25) ratings. The feature launched in early October 2026 after more than a decade of user requests. In less than two days after the launch of half and quarter stars, the Goodreads community added 3.5 million book ratings across the site. The four most-used new star ratings so far are, in order: 3.5, 4.5, 3.75, and 4.25.

However, all of your historic whole-star ratings remain exactly as they were. They will remain unchanged unless you want to go back and re-rate dozens to hundreds of books. Kindle integration allows users to sync or refine their ratings on the Goodreads platform after reading.

The new rating system might be too late for Goodreads. Many people on social media have voiced concerns: “I think ‘why now’ is because enough people have left Goodreads and moved to other reading trackers that it’s finally hurting them, so they’re scrambling to finally implement these features and get people back.”

“I’ve never understood why people were so feral about wanting half-stars. And quarter stars?? That’s just too many. The 5-star system works fine.”

This new system has been a bit buggy from the start. The Goodreads desktop app doesn’t support the new stars yet, but Goodreads hasn’t prioritized it in a long time.

entries.title: Google launched Expert Intelligence on Google Play Books
entries.summary: The platform launched with over 100,000 titles; the integration lets users generate quizzes, infographics, and Audio Overviews while combining published books with personal notes. The post Google launched Expert Intelligence on Google Play Books first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Google launched Expert Intelligence, a cross-product AI initiative that lets you add eligible e-books purchased from Google Play Books directly into Gemini Notebook as grounded sources. The platform launched with over 100,000 titles; the integration lets users generate quizzes, infographics, and Audio Overviews while combining published books with personal notes.

Expert Intelligence launched a month ago with more than 100,000 books from major publishers, including Bloomsbury, De Gruyter Brill, Johns Hopkins University Press, Macmillan Publishers, O’Reilly Media, and Penguin Random House. Google also collaborated closely with more than 15 bestselling authors — including Steven Pinker, Michael Pollan, and Jennifer Wallace — to curate special Featured Notebooks that supplement their books with additional sources and engaging artifacts that let readers dive deeper into the author’s work.

You can see if a book is eligible for Expert Intelligence by visiting Google Play Books. If eligible, you’ll see Gemini Notebook listed when you click the “Tools” badge on a book’s detail page. To get you started, they’re also providing a book for people in the U.S. while supplies last. In the future, people will also be able to add more sources, such as third-party subscriptions, business research reports, and textbooks.

entries.title: Spotify Audiobooks is expanding like crazy in 2026
entries.summary: From now through the end of 2026, Spotify is expanding audiobook access from 22 countries to over 180. The post Spotify Audiobooks is expanding like crazy in 2026 first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Spotify announced it will expand from 22 markets to more than 180 by the end of 2026. More than 750 million people around the globe will soon have the opportunity to stream or purchase books on Spotify. This expansion will let listeners in new markets access an impressive collection of over 350,000 titles, including new catalogs in languages such as Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, and Polish, among others, across more than 120 languages.

“Books change how we see the world, and the people in it,” said Owen Smith, VP of Audiobooks, Spotify. “For a lot of people, audiobooks are how they find their way back to reading, on the commute, on a walk, or at the end of a long day. Bringing audiobooks to more than 180 markets means millions more people can discover that, and authors and publishers can reach readers they’ve never been able to reach before.”

In November, users on a Student plan can use Audiobooks+ to add additional listening hours in Ireland, Belgium, Austria, and Finland. Audiobooks+ lets Spotify Premium users purchase extra audiobook listening time on top of their existing base plan. It also allows members on Premium Family and Duo plans to get 15 hours of audiobook listening a month through a recurring add-on. Since launching just over a year ago, we have more than one million Audiobooks+ subscribers, exceeding $100 million in annual recurring revenue. We plan to extend availability to Student plans in additional markets in the coming year.

The full list of countries is very extensive, and the complete list is available in a recent Spotify Audiobook blog post.

entries.title: Audible will launch in new countries in 2027
entries.summary: Audible will launch localized listener experiences in five new countries next year — Indonesia, South Korea, Denmark, Norway and Finland. The post Audible will launch in new countries in 2027 first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Audible has announced it will launch localized listener experiences in five new countries next year — Indonesia, South Korea, Denmark, Norway and Finland — adding to the 11 new countries announced earlier this year at London Book Fair. Customers in these countries will be able to pay in their local currency and receive recommendations specifically tailored to their region.

Audible Chief Content Officer Rachel Ghiazza said they released a study in conjunction with NielsenIQ titled The Future of Listening. Of the 18,000 listeners surveyed across 11 countries, 34 percent reported consuming more spoken-word audio in the last 12 months than in the year before. The impulse seems rooted in a wish to spend time more beneficially: more than half intentionally replace screen-time entertainment with audio, and 47 percent attribute a reduction in their social media usage to listening. Parents share the sentiment, citing “screen-free entertainment” as the number one reason they encourage kids to listen; 52 percent of parents who are listeners say their children listen, too. And nearly every country ranked relaxing at home as their top listening occasion.

Ghiazza says, “What’s particularly striking about this research is the scale and momentum of audio’s growth. Audio is continuing to play a growing, evolving role in people’s lives. We’re seeing audiences listen more, explore different ways to experience stories, and increasingly turn to audio as a means of switching off and recharging. In today’s world, consumers are craving more fulfilling ways to spend their time, and they’re finding that more and more through audio content, particularly as an alternative to screens.”

As global audiences increasingly consume audio content, the audio format continues to enhance the overall publishing sector: 63 percent of participants reported that after listening to an audiobook by an author, they went on to purchase their works in print or eBook formats. Consumers enjoy interacting with a title in various formats, with 61 percent of audio listeners having also read the book after experiencing it in audio, and 69 percent engaging with audiobooks of titles they had already read in another format. Additionally, audio serves as a pathway for exploration: since diving into audiobooks, listeners have indicated they are discovering new authors (29 percent) and genres (29 percent), and reading more eBooks (26 percent) and physical books (22 percent).

This aligns with what we understand about Audible’s multi-format users: they engage with almost double the amount of content each month compared to those who only listen to audiobooks. Features such as Read & Listen facilitate this type of engagement by integrating a user’s audiobook and eBook into a unified experience: users can read while they listen, alternate between reading and listening without losing their place, and obtain a companion audiobook at a reduced price. Ghiazza announced at the fair that Audible’s Read & Listen features will soon be introduced to seven new markets: Canada, France, Spain, Italy, Brazil, Japan, and India. Initially, titles will be accessible in English and German, with local language versions set to roll out in 2027.

entries.title: Amazon releases new Alexa Tablets
entries.summary: The new Amazon Alexa line of tablets runs Android 16 and has full access to the Play Store, rather than FireOS. The post Amazon releases new Alexa Tablets first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Amazon has quietly announced the 2026 Alexa Tablets, which combine powerful hardware, Alexa+ intelligence, and built-in access to all your favorite apps from the Google Play Store. The lineup includes three models: the Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, the Amazon Alexa Tablet 11, and the Amazon Alexa Tablet 8.

Each new tablet features premium aluminum unibody construction, vivid high-resolution displays, and powerful processors. They seamlessly connect your Amazon experiences right out of the box and run Google Android 16, with Android 17 planned for next year. You can download millions of free and paid apps such as YouTube, Netflix, Gmail, and Google Docs- alongside built-in Amazon apps including Prime Video, Kindle, Audible, Amazon Music, Amazon Quick, and Amazon Luna.

Unlike older Fire tablets that used a custom, forked version of Android (Fire OS) restricted to the Amazon Appstore, these new models run a full version of Android with standard Google services and apps.

Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro

Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is the most advanced tablet we’ve ever built. Stamped from a single piece of aluminum, it measures just 6.5 mm thick, is super lightweight, and is engineered for perfect balance. It houses a 12-inch, 280 PPI display, a 120Hz refresh rate, and a 3:2 aspect ratio for more usable screen space—perfect for reading, watching, or working. The Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro comes in two display options: a vibrant standard display and a cutting-edge Nanomatte display with anti-glare.

Powered by a 4nm 8-core chip with up to 16GB of RAM, the Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro delivers nearly three times faster processing and nine times faster graphics than any tablet we’ve ever shipped—handling everything from multi-window multitasking to graphic-intensive gaming and 4K streaming. With quad Dolby Atmos speakers, Wi-Fi 6E, and 16 hours of video playback—the longest we’ve ever put on a tablet—it provides all-day power. The Nanomatte model goes further, with even more processing power and up to 16GB of RAM.

Amazon Alexa Tablet 11

The new Amazon Alexa Tablet 11—an 11-inch device with a 2.5K display at 276 pixels per inch, 90Hz smooth scrolling, and a 16:10 cinematic aspect ratio—is designed for streaming, gaming, reading, and browsing. A thin aluminum unibody houses an 8-core processor with 8GB of RAM, dual Dolby Atmos speakers, and up to 15 hours of video playback. Alexa+ is built in with the same Dynamic Tab, voice and touch access, and personalized intelligence. Available in Graphite, Amethyst, and Matcha.

Amazon Alexa Tablet 8

The new Amazon Alexa Tablet 8 is the most portable tablet in the lineup, with an 8.7-inch display in an all-aluminum design that weighs just 329g. At 7.95mm thick, it’s designed to fit in one hand and carry anywhere, making it ideal for reading, browsing, and streaming on the go. It’s powered by an 8-core processor with Wi-Fi 6, up to 14 hours of video playback, and built-in Alexa+ intelligence. Available in Graphite, Rosette, and Teal.

How much they cost

Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro (all-new), 8GB RAM, 128GB, 12″ stunning 2.8K display, All-day battery...

Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro (all-new), 16GB RAM, 256GB, 12″ 2.8K Nanomatte display, All-day...

Amazon Alexa Tablet 11 (All-new), 8GB RAM, 128GB, 11″ stunning 2.5K display, All-day battery, With...

Amazon Alexa Tablet 8 (All-new), 4GB RAM, 128GB, 8.7″ compact tablet with vivid display, All-day...

All three Amazon Alexa Tablets will be available for purchase today and will ship on October 14, 2026, in the United States, Mexico, and Canada. They’ll start shipping in the UK, Germany, France, Italy, and Spain on October 19th 2026.

entries.title: The Amazon Kindle 2026 has a light bleed problem
entries.summary: The Amazon Kindle's 2026 model has a flush screen and bezel and suffers from prominent light bleeding in dark mode, which is a defect. The post The Amazon Kindle 2026 has a light bleed problem first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The Amazon Kindle 2026 model, in both plastic and aluminum, now has a flush bezel and a protective glass layer. Many users report that a faint dark or side-LED line can occasionally appear along the bezel edges when the front light is on. This is a hardware defect, so please contact Amazon for a replacement.

Amazon is aware of this issue and admits some current batches of the base Kindle, in all colors, have a problem. This was primarily due to the e-reader’s new construction and how they layered the touchscreen and front-lit display.

They have stated, “While minor edge shadows or side-lighting variations can happen on flush-front e-readers, prominent light bleeding (especially in dark mode) is often considered a defect. Users experiencing severe light bleed on new units are typically advised to exchange the device.”

To contact Amazon, use their live chat to speak with an agent online. Many people have found that Amazon sends a replacement before they send the old unit back. Alternatively, you can phone the Kindle Warranty Support team at 866-321-8851. When you receive the new Kindle, simply sign in with your email address and password, and it will have all the Kindle books you have purchased.

Update: Amazon issued the following statement to Good e-Reader: “When a device is in dark mode with brightness at max in a dark setting, customers may see a glow around the edges of the book. This was expected to achieve a color bezel, and it appears only in very specific use cases, like dark mode with high brightness. If customers want to mitigate this glow, we recommend trying a lower brightness setting when in dark mode.”

entries.content:
Remarkable has just launched a new accessory: the Forest Brown Leather Folio for Remarkable Paper Pure. Crafted from leather in a timeless Forest Brown finish, this premium folio offers elegant wraparound protection while complementing Paper Pure’s minimalist design. Launching ahead of the peak gifting season, it provides a sophisticated upgrade for existing Paper Pure owners and the ideal premium finishing touch for new customers.

The exterior is made from genuine leather in brown and lined with blue microfiber padding, with magnets that wake and lock your device when you remove or insert it. entries.title: The best mini e-readers of 2026
entries.summary: Many new small e-readers are already out or will be available soon; these are the best ones to spend your money on. The post The best mini e-readers of 2026 first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The best mini and pocket-sized e-readers of 2026 balance ultra-portable dimensions with sharp E Ink displays and flexible reading ecosystems. This is a really new product category that has only been picking up steam this year, and many entrants have entered the fray.

Xteink X4 Pro

  • The XTEINK X4 Pro is a highly portable, 4.3-inch pocket e-reader designed as a distraction-free alternative to smartphone doomscrolling. Reviewers from platforms like WIRED praise its featherlight 72-gram body and major hardware upgrades over previous iterations, most notably the addition of a responsive touchscreen and an integrated dual-tone front light with adjustable color temperatures for nighttime reading. To support these power-hungry additions, the manufacturer nearly doubled the battery capacity to 1,100 mAh while maintaining an ultra-thin 5.95 mm profile with built-in magnets for easy phone attachment. This device costs $99 on their website.

Onyx Boox Picco

  • The Onyx BOOX Picco is an ultra-compact, card-sized e-reader that marks a major departure from the brand’s usual Android tablets. Swapping Android for a custom, lightweight Linux-based operating system, this 3.97-inch pocket device ditches the Google Play Store to prioritize a distraction-free, hyper-portable reading experience. Early reviews from platforms like eWritable praise its featherlight 58-gram build and exceptional ergonomics, noting that its tactile, customizable page-turn rocker allows for effortless one-handed use. Unlike some miniature competitors, it includes an integrated adjustable front light that preserves screen depth and contrast, plus a convenient USB-C port and expandable microSD storage up to 2TB. It will retail for $109.99 when it comes out this Fall.

Pocketbook Q

  • PocketBook is launching its Q design e-reader this Fall. The phone-sized e-reader, with a 5.84-inch eye-safe, glare-free E Ink Carta 1300 touchscreen, is designed for everyday reading and listening to audiobooks. Physical side buttons make turning pages effortless with one hand, while the Linux-based platform keeps the experience focused on reading rather than notifications and endless scrolling. The product will be available in late fall for $235.00.

Metalio INK 4

  • The Metalio INK 4is a compact, 3.97-inch pocket-sized E-Ink e-reader and AI companion built with a premium 6mm aluminum alloy frame. It functions as a minimalist hardware device integrated with AI features like a built-in microphone, speaker, and camera, designed to let users sync data to the cloud and decouple from their smartphones. It connects over 4G or Wi-Fi, ships with Baiwen AI chat, a daily checklist, book reading, content transfer, and wallpaper push, and lets you flash the firmware directly from a browser. The device lacks an integrated frontlight for night reading and a gyroscope for automatic screen rotation.

It retails for $72.00 on AliExpress.

entries.title: Rakuten Kobo is now selling bundle sets
entries.summary: Rakuten Kobo now sells e-reader bundles that include a case, Kobo Remote, and 5 free e-books from Sarah J. Maas's ACOTAR series. The post Rakuten Kobo is now selling bundle sets first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Rakuten Kobo used to sell e-readers and accessories, such as cases and their Remote Bluetooth page-turner. The company has just started selling bundle sets on their website. They have various Libra Color bundles, Kobo Clara Color, and Kobo Clara BW. All come with five free e-books from the ACOTAR series by Sarah J. Maas.

The Kobo Libra Color bundle is very expensive. You get a Remote, 3 different color cases, and a Kobo Pencil 2. This bundle costs $399, while the e-reader on its own is $259. There are two bundles; the only difference is the e-reader color: black or white.  The Kobo Clara Color Bundle also comes in two colors and includes a case and the Kobo Remote; this bundle costs $239, while the e-reader alone is $179. The Kobo BW has the same bundle as the Clara color. However, the bundle price is $219, while the regular price is $159.

Most people who buy e-readers and have them out in the wild don’t normally buy cases. I see people all over Vancouver, BC, using Kindles on the SkyTrain, buses, or just out in public, and I can’t remember the last time I saw someone with a case. I suppose some people like cases so they don’t damage the display while carrying them in a crowded handbag, purse, or messenger bag.

Rakuten Kobo did not publicly announce the new bundle deals, along with the five free e-books, on social media, nor did it issue a press release.

entries.title: How to Listen to Kindle Books With CastReader
entries.summary: A practical guide to connecting your Kindle library on a phone or tablet and reading aloud in Kindle Cloud Reader on a computer. The post How to Listen to Kindle Books With CastReader first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
A practical guide to connecting your Kindle library on a phone or tablet and reading aloud in Kindle Cloud Reader on a computer.

You are three chapters into a Kindle book, but the rest of the evening involves making dinner rather than sitting down to read. Text to speech lets you listen to the same book, then return to the screen whenever you want to check a passage.

CastReader offers two routes. On an iPhone, iPad, Android phone or Android tablet, its mobile app can connect to your Kindle library and synchronize your bookshelf. On a computer, its browser extension works with Kindle Cloud Reader. The preparation differs, so start with the route that matches your device.

Choose the mobile app for phones and tablets, or the browser extension for Kindle Cloud Reader on a computer.

What Kindle text to speech can and cannot replace

A professionally produced audiobook includes a narrator’s interpretation of the writing. Text to speech generates spoken audio from readable text. It gives you a choice of voices and playback speeds, but not necessarily distinct performances for every character or an actor’s handling of unfamiliar names.

Neither format has to replace the other. An audiobook may be preferable for a particular performance; TTS is useful when you mainly want to continue reading. CastReader does not supply access to the book itself. You still need your own Amazon account and permission to read the title.

Before you begin

Choose a book that already opens normally in your Kindle reading service. Check a familiar chapter first, rather than discovering an account or access problem halfway through setting up narration. Availability can vary by book, account and region.

Use the mobile app on phones and tablets, or the Chrome or Edge extension on a computer. Installing a desktop extension is not a step you can simply repeat inside the Kindle mobile app. A familiar passage also makes it easier to notice missed lines or awkward page transitions.

Connect your Kindle bookshelf on a phone or tablet

Install the app. Visit the CastReader mobile app page and follow the link to the appropriate official app store. Open the installed app. Interface details can differ between platforms and releases, so follow the prompts in your version.

Connect your own Kindle library. Find Kindle among the reading services or bookshelf options and complete the account connection shown on screen. This brings your existing reading access into the workflow; it does not give other people access to your books.

Let the bookshelf synchronize and open a title. A cover appearing in the library is only the starting point. Open the book and check that the intended chapter displays correctly before starting narration.

Select Read Aloud and an available voice. Begin at a comfortable, ordinary speed. Listen to a few paragraphs before increasing it. Synchronized highlighting and automatic scrolling help you find the current passage when you want to look back at the text.

Check pause and resume before a longer session. The mobile workflow supports background listening, lock screen playback and resuming. Try these within one chapter first. Notice what happens when you leave the app, receive an interruption or change networks, rather than discovering the behavior during a long listening session.

For bedtime reading, check whether your version offers a sleep timer. It can prevent playback continuing far beyond the point where you fell asleep. These are CastReader reading controls, not a promise that every position will synchronize perfectly with all your Amazon devices.

Listen in Kindle Cloud Reader on a computer

Install the extension. Follow the Kindle browser listening guide to the official Chrome or Edge extension listing. Make sure the extension is enabled and has permission to work on the relevant reading page.

Open Kindle Cloud Reader. Go to read.amazon.com in your browser, sign in to your own Amazon account and open a book you can access there. Wait for the text to appear. If the book itself will not open, resolve that before troubleshooting narration.

Start CastReader and choose narration. Use the reading control on the page or the extension entry point, then select a voice and play. Button locations can change; the important check is whether CastReader recognizes the current page correctly.

Watch the first page transition. Listen to a few paragraphs and follow the move to the next page. If you hear repetition or a skipped passage, pause, find a clear starting point in the text and resume. Illustrated pages and extensive footnotes need more attention than straightforward prose.

The desktop workflow recognizes text from the visible reading page and sends the text needed for narration into the speech workflow. It is not a Kindle file downloader, exporter or protection removal tool. Continuous reading also depends on the accessibility and compatibility of the current page.

Make listening part of reading

Match your approach to the book. A familiar novel may work well alongside simple chores. A new story with many characters is easier to follow if you keep the text nearby initially. With nonfiction, pause at an important claim and look back at how the author supports it.

Maps, diagrams, poetry and dense footnotes are good reasons to switch back to the screen. Narration communicates words, not every relationship expressed by their layout. Moving between looking and listening is a useful reading habit; you do not have to stay away from the screen for the whole chapter.

Choose Read Aloud when you want the author’s text. Where supported, AI Explain can help you approach an unfamiliar argument, but its explanation reorganizes the material. It is not a substitute for the complete original or an exact quotation.

Understand the offline option

Current iOS release notes describe saving a Kindle book through the player’s More menu, finding it under Offline Books in settings and using a system voice for offline narration. That does not mean cloud AI voices or AI Explain work without an internet connection. It also does not establish equivalent offline support on Android or desktop.

Before a flight or unreliable connection, save the content in your installed version and test a short passage with the network disconnected. Confirm that the book, voice and reading position are available. A cached cover alone does not establish that you can listen offline.

Troubleshoot in a useful order

A book is missing. Check that you connected the correct account and can access the title in the original reading service. Then try the refresh or reconnection options available in the app.

The book opens but narration will not start. Wait for the body text to load and check the network and selected voice. On desktop, also check extension activation and permission for the current website.

Reading stops or repeats after a page turn. Find the point in the original text, pause and restart from there. Check for app or extension updates. Recent mobile updates include continuity, page transition and recovery fixes, but an individual book still needs testing.

A name sounds wrong. Check the language and voice, then try another voice or a more suitable speed. Return to the text if pronunciation affects your understanding; a generated reading is not an authority on how a name should sound.

Try your own book before choosing a plan

CastReader provides a free daily allowance. Pro expands access to standard narration and AI Explain. Website pricing is US$4.99 monthly or US$35.99 billed annually; app store pricing, region and taxes can differ. A subscription does not include the book’s purchase price or reading rights.

For occasional listening, the free option provides a starting point. Before subscribing for longer sessions, check whether your own book reads continuously, resumes reliably and sounds comfortable over a chapter. The aim is simple: give a book you already want to read another place in your day.

Markus lives in San Francisco, California and is the video game and audio expert on Good e-Reader! He has a huge interest in new e-readers and tablets, and gaming.
